extracted.intended_audience: students using the Software Foundations / Rocq textbook (learning Gallina/Rocq and submitting homework)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidelines and correctness criteria for writing, testing, and submitting Solutions to the 'Basics: Functional Programming in Rocq' chapter (Gallina/Rocq definitions, examples, and proofs), plus how the autograder interprets submissions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not change exercise names
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not change the names of exercises. Otherwise the grading scripts will be unable to find your solution.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Keep all exercise identifiers exactly as given in the .v file so autograder/test scripts can locate and evaluate your solutions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not delete exercises; partial proofs allowed
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not delete exercises. If you skip an exercise (e.g., because it is marked 'optional,' or because you can't solve it), it is OK to leave a partial proof in your .v file; in this case, please make sure it ends with the keyword Admitted (not, for example, Abort).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Leaving a placeholder using Admitted is acceptable for skipped/unfinished exercises; do not remove the exercise declaration itself.

rubrics_metrics.name: Helper definitions allowed and placement
rubrics_metrics.description: It is fine to use additional definitions (of helper functions, useful lemmas, etc.) in your solutions. You can put these before the theorem you are asked to prove.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Helper functions and lemmas may precede the stated exercise; they can be used to simplify proofs and implementations, but be careful about leaving unproven helpers (see Admitted guidance).

rubrics_metrics.name: Admitted as placeholder; impact on grading
rubrics_metrics.description: The Admitted command can be used as a placeholder for an incomplete proof. We use it in exercises to indicate the parts that we're leaving for you -- i.e., your job is to replace Admitteds with real proofs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If you introduce a helper lemma that you end up being unable to prove, hence end it with Admitted, then make sure to also end the main theorem in which you use it with Admitted, not Qed. This will make sure you get partial credit if you use that main theorem to solve a later exercise. Beware: every time you say Admitted you are leaving a door open for total nonsense to enter Rocq's safe, formally checked world!

rubrics_metrics.name: File submission rules (general)
rubrics_metrics.description: There is no need to hand in BasicsTest.v itself (or Preface.v). If your class is using the Canvas system to hand in assignments... If you submit multiple versions of the assignment, you may notice that they are given different names. This is fine: The most recent submission is the one that will be graded. If you are handing in multiple files at the same time (i.e., if more than one chapter is assigned in the same week), you should make a single submission with all the files at once by using the 'Add another file' button just above the comment box.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Don't submit internal test files; when multiple files are required, place them in a single submission; instructors/Canvas will normally grade the most recent upload.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use the provided test scripts to check formatting and grading
rubrics_metrics.description: Each chapter (e.g., Basics.v) is accompanied by a test script (e.g., BasicsTest.v) that automatically calculates points for the finished homework problems in the chapter. To run it, make sure you have saved Basics.v to disk. Then first run rocq compile -Q . LF Basics.v and then run rocq compile -Q . LF BasicsTest.v; or, if you have make installed, you can run make BasicsTest.vo.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Run the provided test scripts locally before submitting to verify that your file is well formatted and that examples/theorems are discoverable by autograder. Use the test output to debug missing exercises or formatting issues.

rubrics_metrics.name: Interpreting autograder/test script output
rubrics_metrics.description: The test script output: First will be all the output produced by Basics.v itself. Second, for each required exercise, there is a report that tells you its point value (the number of stars or some fraction thereof if there are multiple parts to the exercise), whether its type is ok, and what assumptions it relies upon. If the type is not ok, it means you proved the wrong thing: most likely, you accidentally modified the theorem statement while you were proving it. The assumptions are any unproved theorems which your solution relies upon. 'Closed under the global context' means 'none'. Third, you will see the maximum number of points in standard and advanced versions of the assignment (based on stars). Fourth, you will see a list of 'Allowed Axioms'. Finally, you will see a summary of whether you have solved each exercise. Exercises that are manually graded will also show up in the output.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Check (1) that each exercise's type is ok (you didn't change the statement), (2) that assumptions do not include unexpected axioms (unless allowed), and (3) the allowed-axioms list; use this output to confirm which exercises passed and why.

rubrics_metrics.name: If 'type is not ok' you proved the wrong statement
rubrics_metrics.description: If the type is not ok, it means you proved the wrong thing: most likely, you accidentally modified the theorem statement while you were proving it. The autograder won't give you any points in this case, so make sure to correct the theorem.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Always preserve the original theorem/exercise statement; do not alter the statement when proving it.

rubrics_metrics.name: Allowed axioms in autograder
rubrics_metrics.description: The test script lists 'Allowed Axioms'. These are unproven theorems that your solution is permitted to depend upon, aside from the fundamental axioms of Rocq's logic. You'll probably see something about functional_extensionality for this chapter; we'll cover what that means in a later chapter.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be aware of which axioms are permitted; solutions depending on other axioms will be flagged in the assumptions list in test output.

rubrics_metrics.name: Examples / unit tests must be verifiable in Rocq
rubrics_metrics.description: Example declarations make assertions and give the assertion a name. Having made the assertion, we can also ask Rocq to verify it using a Proof script (e.g., simpl; reflexivity; Qed). The Examples in the chapter are 'unit tests' and constitute a complete specification (e.g., a truth table for orb). The exercises include Example tests that 'should pass'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Implement functions so that the provided Example proofs succeed under Rocq (use simpl and reflexivity or other tactics as appropriate). Filling in Example proofs is part of correctness checking.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer explicit type annotations in definitions for readability
rubrics_metrics.description: Note that the argument and return types of this function are explicitly declared on the first line. Like most functional programming languages, Rocq can often figure out these types for itself when they are not given explicitly -- i.e., it can do type inference -- but we'll generally include them to make reading easier.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Although not required, include type annotations on definitions to help human readers and reduce surprises.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use Notation and modules to improve readability and avoid name collisions
rubrics_metrics.description: Notation commands define readable infix syntax for existing definitions. The Module/End markers allow scoping so that definitions inside a module are referred to as X.foo outside it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Introduce notations for common operations and use modules (Module ... End) to limit scope so you can reuse names safely.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recommended proof patterns and tactic behavior
rubrics_metrics.description: Common tactics: intros (to move quantifiers/hypotheses into the context), simpl (to simplify terms), reflexivity (checks equality, does some simplification/unfolding), rewrite (to replace using an equality hypothesis or theorem), destruct (case analysis; supports 'as [| n'] eqn:E' patterns, creating subgoals). Reflexivity can sometimes do more unfolding than simpl. Use destruct to consider constructor cases and provide eqn: annotations to name the equations introduced.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Follow the patterns shown in examples: intros ...; simpl; reflexivity for simple equalities; use rewrite H to replace occurrences using hypothesis H; use destruct with intro patterns and eqn: to do case analysis with clear documentation of assumptions in subgoals.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of Compute and Check for experimentation and types
rubrics_metrics.description: Three ways to do examples: Compute evaluates an expression; Example records an expected result and can be proved; extract can generate OCaml/Haskell/Scheme code. The Check command asks Rocq to print the type of an expression (or verify it against an expected type when followed by : type).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use Compute to experiment interactively, Example+Proof to state and verify unit tests, and Check to confirm types of expressions, functions, and theorems.

rubrics_metrics.name: Star-based point scheme
rubrics_metrics.description: For each required exercise, the report tells you its point value (the number of stars or some fraction thereof if there are multiple parts to the exercise). The maximum number of points in standard and advanced versions of the assignment is shown; that number is based on the number of stars in the non-optional exercises.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the star counts in the chapter to estimate exercise weight; autograder aggregates points accordingly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Autograder 'assumptions' indicate unproven dependencies
rubrics_metrics.description: The 'assumptions' listed by the test script are any unproved theorems which your solution relies upon. 'Closed under the global context' means none: you have solved the exercise. On the other hand, a list of axioms means you haven't fully solved the exercise.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Aim for solutions that are closed under the global context (no unpermitted assumptions); if assumptions appear, inspect which lemmas/theorems were left Admitted or which axioms were introduced.
